independence_scope: intra-mesh Anthropic-family; agreement is corroboration, never cross-provider evidence

reviews.reasoning: Re-derived numbering first: web_mt_offset_map.json makes Ps 144 an identity psalm (rule 'identity', mt_title_verses [], 15 WEB verses / 15 MT verses), so ps_lib.web_to_mt sends web:Ps.144.1-4 to oshb:Ps.144.1-4 with no offset and no dual-cite obligation; the title pseudo-ref pairing web:Ps.144.0 = oshb:Ps.144.1 is the owner-ruled form and citation_sweep.py returns GREEN on the row. Every Hebrew run in the row collates at BYTE tier against its cited ref (collate.py): the title word against oshb:Ps.144.1, the blessing splice against oshb:Ps.144.1, the four-epithet splice against oshb:Ps.144.2, and the what-is-man splice against oshb:Ps.144.3. The WEB quotes are verbatim (check_web_quotes.py GREEN on this row; the em dash closing web:Ps.144.1 is simply not carried into the quote, which is a prefix match). check_refs_mirror.py and check_marks.py are GREEN, and check_tiling.py tiles Ps.144.1-Ps.144.15 exactly across the four rows of this psalm. The trailing boundary at 4|5 holds on both witnesses: MT 144:5 opens a vocative plus imperative sequence and carries the span's first 2ms suffix token, and WEB reads “Part your heavens, Yahweh, and come down.” (web:Ps.144.5). What does not hold is the row's account of the person frame INSIDE the span, which is asserted twice (rationale: 'without changing addressee'; rejected_alternative: 'both remain second-person address to Yahweh with no imperative or addressee change') and is the entire stated ground for refusing the 1-2 | 3-4 rival. That is challenge OL-472-1. A second, smaller defect: the paseq signal reports a POSITION the staged inventory cannot carry (OL-472-2); its count is right. Observations, not challenges: the Ps 18 relation in device_notes is argued in English only, though it is quantifiable in the bytes — MT 144:1-2 and oshb:Ps.18.3 (= web:Ps.18.2) share 5 epithet tokens at skeleton tier besides the divine name (6 shared skeleton tokens in all), and the phrase behind “He teaches my hands to war” (web:Ps.18.34 = oshb:Ps.18.35) is a skeleton substring of MT 144:1, which the row could have cited instead of leaving a tier-1-flavoured echo on English alone. check_universals.py flags the rejected_alternative's imperative-absence claim as unswept; the claim is in fact true for MT 144:1-4, but no digit-bearing sweep is possible for it, since the staged extract has no morphology layer. Confidence 'high' is over-calibrated given that the row's only rival-rejection argument is factually inverted.

challenges.claim: The row's rationale and rejected_alternative both assert that web:Ps.144.1-2 and web:Ps.144.3-4 are alike second-person address to Yahweh with no addressee change, but MT 144:1-2 carries no second-person form at all and marks God in the third person, while MT 144:3 carries two second-person forms plus a fresh vocative — so the tier-1 addressee signal falls exactly on the 2|3 seam the row dismisses.
challenges.evidence: Person census over the span, byte-spliced from verse_map_oshb.json and counted per word token: MT 144:1 has 9 word tokens and MT 144:2 has 11 (20 tokens across the two verses); exactly 1 of those 20 ends in final kaf, and it is בָּ֘ר֤וּךְ (oshb:Ps.144.1), a passive participle, not a 2ms suffix; second-person suffix or prefix forms in MT 144:1-2: 0. The one explicit pronoun for God in MT 144:2 is third person — וּב֣וֹ חָסִ֑יתִי (oshb:Ps.144.2, collate.py tier byte) — and WEB agrees: “my shield, and he in whom I take refuge, who subdues my people under me.” (web:Ps.144.2), against the third-person opening “Blessed be Yahweh, my rock, who trains my hands to war” (web:Ps.144.1). MT 144:3 by contrast opens יְֽהוָ֗ה מָה אָ֭דָם (oshb:Ps.144.3, tier byte) — vocative first — and carries 2 second-person wayyiqtol forms of its 7 word tokens, וַתֵּדָעֵ֑הוּ and וַֽתְּחַשְּׁבֵֽהוּ (oshb:Ps.144.3, both tier byte), which WEB renders “Yahweh, what is man, that you care for him? Or the son of man, that you think of him?” (web:Ps.144.3). Second-person tokens by sub-span in MT 144: vv1-2 = 0, v3 = 2, v4 = 0. The rejected_alternative's premise is therefore false in both witnesses, and the signal it denies (a third-person-to-second-person addressee shift plus a new vocative at the 2|3 seam) is precisely a tier-1 speech-frame signal for the rival split it was written to defeat. The span Ps.144.1-4 may still be defensible on other grounds, but not on this one: the rival must be defeated by an argument that survives the bytes.

challenges.claim: The paseq signal attributes a placement ('touching the title-adjacent words') to the marks inventory, which records paseq as a per-verse COUNT only and carries no positional data; the count of two is correct, the placement is unsupported by any staged evidence.
challenges.evidence: pmarks_Ps.json paseq is a verse-keyed count map — its Ps 144 entries are Ps.144.1 = 2 and Ps.144.12 = 1 (481 verses in the inventory) — with the note 'Seg layer, NOT quotable verse bytes; citable from this inventory only.' No offsets, no word indices. Nor can the verse bytes supply them: U+05C0 occurs 0 times across all 2527 MT verses of the staged extract, and 0 times in the full byte-true text of that verse, לְדָוִ֨ד בָּ֘ר֤וּךְ יְהוָ֨ה צוּרִ֗י הַֽמְלַמֵּ֣ד יָדַ֣י לַקְרָ֑ב אֶ֝צְבְּעוֹתַ֗י לַמִּלְחָמָֽה (oshb:Ps.144.1, collate.py tier byte). The count claim is sound and correctly disclosed as single-witness seg layer; only the positional gloss exceeds what the inventory can license.

reviews.reasoning: Both seams verify on both witnesses. At 4|5 the row is right that a fresh petition opens: MT 144:5 begins with the vocative and the imperative, and carries the first of 3 second-person suffix tokens in MT 144:5-8 — שָׁמֶ֣יךָ (oshb:Ps.144.5), חִ֝צֶּ֗יךָ (oshb:Ps.144.6) and יָדֶ֗יךָ (oshb:Ps.144.7), each collate.py tier byte, 3 tokens across the 4 verses against 0 in MT 144:3-4. At 8|9 the seam is stronger than the row argues: MT 144:9 opens with the psalm's only unsuffixed Elohim noun token, אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים (oshb:Ps.144.9, collate.py tier byte), where the psalm's other four divine-name tokens all carry the tetragrammaton — MT 144:1, 3, 5 and 15, the last of them under a relative prefix — a divine-name switch riding the row's own closing boundary, which the row does not claim and did not need. Every Hebrew run collates at BYTE tier against its cited ref: the imperative splice against oshb:Ps.144.5 and the rescue splice against oshb:Ps.144.7. WEB quotes are verbatim (check_web_quotes.py raises nothing on this row); citation_sweep.py, check_refs_mirror.py, check_marks.py and check_tiling.py are GREEN. The rejected_alternative is accurate: MT 144:9 has no imperative, its two verbs are first-person, and its addressee marker is the 2ms pronoun repeated twice (לָּ֑ךְ and לָּֽךְ, oshb:Ps.144.9, both tier byte) — a vow, not a petition. Two observations that do not rise to challenges. First, the four-item echo list in observed_substrate_signals is 3-for-4 against the window it names: parted heavens answers “He bowed the heavens also, and came down.” (web:Ps.18.9), scattered lightning answers “He sent out his arrows, and scattered them.” (web:Ps.18.14) and many waters answers “He drew me out of many waters.” (web:Ps.18.16), but nothing in web:Ps.18.9-web:Ps.18.16 smokes or is a mountain — the nearest material is “The foundations also of the mountains quaked” (web:Ps.18.7) and “Smoke went out of his nostrils.” (web:Ps.18.8), both outside the cited window and never combined. Second, the label 'many-waters' is applied to web:Ps.144.7, where WEB in fact reads “deliver me out of great waters” (web:Ps.144.7); the echo is real but it lives in the Hebrew, not the English — מִמַּ֣יִם רַבִּ֑ים (oshb:Ps.144.7, tier byte) matches the corresponding phrase of web:Ps.18.16 = oshb:Ps.18.17 at SKELETON tier only (the accents differ), which is a tier the row never names. Neither point disturbs the span or either seam, so the verdict is support.

The span is right and its opening seam is well founded: MT 144:9 opens the psalm's only Elohim vocative and a first-person vow, and MT 144:11 ends the last petition before the 1cp prosperity material begins. All three Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier against their cited refs (oshb:Ps.144.9, oshb:Ps.144.10, oshb:Ps.144.11), the WEB quotes are verbatim, and citation_sweep.py, check_refs_mirror.py, check_marks.py all return GREEN; the out-of-span verses argued in prose (web:Ps.144.7, web:Ps.144.8, web:Ps.18.50) are all mirrored in boundary_evidence_refs. Confidence 'medium' is appropriately calibrated. Two defects, both in how the evidence is characterised rather than in the span. The repetition signal claims a byte check that does not hold and a word order that is not in fact unchanged (OL-474-1) — and it misses the one byte-identical string the psalm actually offers, which would have carried the same warrant without overstatement. The rationale also types web:Ps.144.10 as third-person description against the reading of the witness it cites (OL-474-2). Observation: the cross-psalm relation to web:Ps.18.50 is again asserted in English only; the shared element is the name David, which is a lexeme claim the row could have byte-anchored on both sides.

challenges.claim: The signal's parenthetical 'byte-checked, the word order recurs unchanged across web:Ps.144.7 and web:Ps.144.11' fails at byte tier for both repeated elements and is false as a word-order claim, since MT 144:11 omits a whole phrase that stands between them in MT 144:7.
challenges.evidence: Paired imperatives: the pair reads פְּצֵ֣נִי וְ֭הַצִּילֵנִי (oshb:Ps.144.7) against פְּצֵ֥נִי וְהַצִּילֵנִי֮ (oshb:Ps.144.11), both byte-spliced from verse_map_oshb.json and each collating at tier byte against its OWN ref. Cross-collated, the highest matching tier between them is accent_stripped — byte and nfd both fail, because the accents differ on both words. Foreigners phrase: מִ֝יַּ֗ד בְּנֵ֣י נֵכָֽר (oshb:Ps.144.7) against מִיַּ֪ד בְּֽנֵי נֵ֫כָ֥ר (oshb:Ps.144.11); these match at SKELETON tier only — accent_stripped also fails here, because MT 144:11 retains a meteg that MT 144:7 does not, and accent_stripped strips cantillation only. Word order: MT 144:7 has 10 word tokens and MT 144:11 has 12; MT 144:7 places מִמַּ֣יִם רַבִּ֑ים (oshb:Ps.144.7, tier byte) between the imperative pair and the foreigners phrase, and MT 144:11 has no counterpart to it, running the imperatives straight into the foreigners phrase. WEB shows the same omission: “rescue me, and deliver me out of great waters, out of the hands of foreigners,” (web:Ps.144.7) against “Rescue me, and deliver me out of the hands of foreigners,” (web:Ps.144.11). The byte-true identity the row could have cited is a different pairing: the whole of that verse, אֲשֶׁ֣ר פִּ֭יהֶם דִּבֶּר שָׁ֑וְא וִֽ֝ימִינָ֗ם יְמִ֣ין שָֽׁקֶר (oshb:Ps.144.8), is byte-identical to the last 7 word tokens of MT 144:11 — collate.py returns tier byte for that same string against oshb:Ps.144.11 — including the relative particle, which is byte-identical between MT 144:8 and MT 144:11. Repairing the signal means naming that pairing and its tier, and demoting the imperative pair to accent_stripped and the foreigners phrase to skeleton.

challenges.claim: The rationale types web:Ps.144.10 as 'third-person description of the divine king-maker', but MT 144:10 has no finite verb and no divine pronoun — only two articular participles — and the witness the row cites renders the verse as continued second-person address, which the row's own rejected_alternative also asserts.
challenges.evidence: MT 144:10's two divine descriptors are הַנּוֹתֵ֥ן and הַ֭פּוֹצֶה (oshb:Ps.144.10, each collate.py tier byte): both are articular participles, and the verse carries 0 second-person suffix tokens and 0 finite third-person verbs. The staged extract has no morphology layer (verse_map_oshb.json carries text/language/web only), so person cannot be machine-derived here; the available witness evidence runs the other way. WEB reads the verse as address continued from the vow: “You are he who gives salvation to kings, who rescues David, his servant, from the deadly sword.” (web:Ps.144.10) — and the row quotes only the relative tail of that sentence, dropping the second-person predication that opens it. Second-person marking is in fact continuous into this verse's context: MT 144:9 carries the 2ms pronoun twice, לָּ֑ךְ and לָּֽךְ (oshb:Ps.144.9, both tier byte). The rationale's 'moving to third-person description' also contradicts the row's own rejected_alternative, which states that no addressee or mode shift separates these verses.

reviews.reasoning: The span itself survives review: Ps.144.12-15 is a coherent closing unit, the psalm ends there, check_tiling.py confirms the four rows tile Ps.144.1-Ps.144.15 with no gap or overlap, and both Hebrew runs collate at BYTE tier against oshb:Ps.144.12 and oshb:Ps.144.15. The closing claim is sound: MT 144:15 carries the beatitude word twice, אַשְׁרֵ֣י and אַֽשְׁרֵ֥י (oshb:Ps.144.15, each tier byte), doubled inside the one verse as the row says — they are not byte-identical to each other (the second adds a meteg and takes a different accent), but the row claims only doubling, not identity, so no defect there. What fails is the opening-seam warrant. Both of the row's start-side statements assert syntactic subordination to web:Ps.144.11, which no staged evidence supports and which WEB contradicts (OL-475-1); and because the row offers nothing else for its start boundary, the strongest tier-1 signal at 11|12 goes unnamed. The row also lets verbatim WEB text out in single curly quotes, which the shared quote checker treats as delimiter evasion (OL-475-2). Observation: 'untroubled oxen' is not what web:Ps.144.14 says of the oxen — WEB reads “Our oxen will pull heavy loads.” (web:Ps.144.14), and the untroubled material in that verse is about the streets, not the herd. check_universals.py also flags the second signal's 'no further imperative or petition following it'; the claim is trivially true because MT 144:15 is the psalm's last verse, but it is unswept as written.

challenges.claim: The row's only start-boundary warrant is the claim that web:Ps.144.12 opens 'as a purpose clause' that 'grammatically continues the petition of web:Ps.144.11 rather than starting an independent clause' — a syntactic determination the staged extract cannot support and that WEB's own rendering contradicts, while the genuine tier-1 signal at the 11|12 seam, a first-person singular to first-person plural speaker shift, is never named.
challenges.evidence: The particle is אֲשֶׁ֤ר (oshb:Ps.144.12, collate.py tier byte). The same particle occurs twice more in this psalm, אֲשֶׁ֣ר (oshb:Ps.144.8) and אֲשֶׁ֣ר (oshb:Ps.144.11) — 3 tokens in Ps 144 in all — and those two are byte-identical to each other while the 144:12 token differs from them at byte tier and matches only at skeleton tier. In both of those verses WEB renders the particle as a relative bound to the foreigners: “whose mouths speak deceit, whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” (web:Ps.144.8). At web:Ps.144.12 WEB does the opposite of what the row claims and opens a new independent sentence: “Then our sons will be like well-nurtured plants, our daughters like pillars carved to adorn a palace.” (web:Ps.144.12). The staged extract has no morphology layer, so neither 'purpose' nor 'relative' is machine-derivable; the label is unsupported in one witness and refuted in the other. Meanwhile the seam has a byte-true tier-1 warrant the row does not use: first-person plural suffix tokens number 7 across MT 144:12-14 — בָּנֵ֨ינוּ, בְּנוֹתֵ֥ינוּ (oshb:Ps.144.12), מְזָוֵ֣ינוּ, צֹאונֵ֣נוּ, בְּחוּצוֹתֵֽינוּ (oshb:Ps.144.13), אַלּוּפֵ֗ינוּ, בִּרְחֹבֹתֵֽינוּ (oshb:Ps.144.14) — against 0 such tokens in MT 144:1-11, whose single word ending in that sequence, וְֽיֶעֱשָֽׁנוּ (oshb:Ps.144.5, tier byte), is verbal, rendered “Touch the mountains, and they will smoke.” (web:Ps.144.5). 7 tokens against 0 is the speaker shift that carries this boundary; the continuity claim the row files instead argues against its own seam without disclosing that it does.

challenges.claim: observed_substrate_signals[1] carries verbatim WEB text in single curly quotes next to a web: ref, which the campaign's quote convention reserves for review-packet prose and the shared checker classifies as delimiter evasion.
challenges.evidence: check_web_quotes.py, run over this cluster's rows, returns flag_count 1, path [3].observed_substrate_signals[1], quote 'Happy are the people', issue 'verbatim WEB text in SINGLE curly quotes (delimiter evasion — rows use double curly + inline web: ref)'. The span is verbatim WEB: “Happy are the people who are in such a situation. Happy are the people whose God is Yahweh.” (web:Ps.144.15). It is not nested inside a double-curly WEB quote, so the checker's WEB-internal-speech exemption does not apply. The same signal already carries an inline web: ref, so the repair is the delimiter alone. Every other WEB quote in this cluster's four rows passes the checker.
